lectures.title: Permissioned Distributed Ledgers For Blockchain - slides
Permissioned Distributed Ledgers For Blockchain - assigned reading

questions.question_stem: A shipping consortium includes competing carriers, ports, insurers, and a regulator. They need a shared handoff record, but no single company should be able to rewrite history. Which design best fits the lesson's tradeoff framework?
questions.correct_answer: A permissioned distributed ledger, because known organizations can share append-only records while distributing administrative authority.
incorrect_answers: A centralized mutable database, because one trusted host can coordinate state changes and resolve competing disputes for every member neutrally.
A permissionless public blockchain, because open miners and economic Sybil resistance are required to coordinate competing enterprise nodes.
An offline hash-linked audit log, because local proof chaining removes dynamic ordering protocols and shared governance controls from the process.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames permissioned ledgers as a fit for cooperating competitors: participants are known, but administrative control and audit evidence should not belong to one unilateral owner.

questions.question_stem: What changes when a ledger uses curated admission instead of open participation?
questions.correct_answer: The system accepts front-loaded identity vetting and role assignment in exchange for stronger accountability among known participants.
incorrect_answers: The system bypasses runtime validation and governance structures because all known members are guaranteed to behave honestly.
The system must enforce resource-heavy proof-of-work consensus because curated admission makes Sybil attacks easier for outsiders to coordinate.
The system acts as a private database because a single administrative owner is required to authorize every state transition.
questions.explanation: Curated admission shifts the security problem from open Sybil resistance to identity management, policy, and institutional accountability.

questions.question_stem: A student says, "Permissioned ledgers do not have Sybil risks because every participant is invited." What is the best correction?
questions.correct_answer: Sybil risk can reappear if identity administration is compromised or weak enough to create unauthorized identities.
incorrect_answers: Sybil risk is eliminated completely because validator nodes are required to use resource-heavy proof-of-work consensus.
Sybil risk only impacts public blockchains and is unrelated to identity management systems and credential authorizations.
Sybil risk disappears once private transaction payloads are cryptographically hidden from other consortium members entirely.
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly warns that named membership only helps if the identity and credential control plane is governed and operated correctly.

questions.question_stem: Which sequence best matches the lesson's generic permissioned-ledger transaction path?
questions.correct_answer: Identity check, proposal, required approvals, ordering, validation, then commit.
incorrect_answers: Open mining, longest-chain consensus, probabilistic confirmation, then validation.
Commit, identity check, arbitrary ordering, proposal, then admin approval.
Proposal, client commit, optional ordering, then validator override when needed.
questions.explanation: The lesson describes a permissioned transaction path in which identity and approvals precede ordering, and deterministic validation precedes commit.

questions.question_stem: A consortium lets the same node both decide transaction order and provide the only required business approval for asset transfers. What security concern does this raise?
questions.correct_answer: It weakens role separation by concentrating sequencing and approval power in one place.
incorrect_answers: It prevents deterministic finality by requiring anonymous miners to sequence blocks.
It enhances accountability by limiting the number of organizations that inspect state.
It eliminates governance risk by allowing one node to dictate policy execution.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes role separation among clients, validators, orderers, admins, and auditors so that no single role quietly accumulates excessive power.

questions.question_stem: Why can a permissioned ledger often treat a transaction as final once the configured quorum or ordering process commits it?
questions.correct_answer: Known membership lets the system use CFT or BFT-style agreement rules that provide deterministic rather than probabilistic finality.
incorrect_answers: Curated admission guarantees the network will never experience hardware faults or malicious node behavior after deployment.
Consensus rules force local peers to wait for multiple public proof-of-work confirmations before finalizing their local state commits.
State distribution requires every participant node to be capable of reordering and resolving forks if consensus splits the network later.
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts permissioned deterministic finality with public-chain probabilistic finality, where confidence usually increases after additional confirmations.

questions.question_stem: A governance committee approves a bad policy that lets an insider enroll unauthorized validators. What does the lesson imply about the ledger's cryptography?
questions.correct_answer: The cryptography may still faithfully enforce the bad policy, so governance failure can compromise the system despite strong primitives.
incorrect_answers: Strong mathematical cryptography automatically detects and overrides any unfair policy decisions that do not match the network consensus rules.
Hash-linked ledger records erase unauthorized validator activities as soon as their enrollment becomes unpopular with other member firms.
Deterministic finality protects the network by rendering internal committee governance decisions and policy updates completely non-binding.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats governance as an attack surface: a blockchain records and enforces what its rules allow, even when those rules are poorly governed.

questions.question_stem: A permissioned network still exists, but no one can add members, rotate keys, or update channels because the required admin certificates expired. What lesson concept best explains this outage?
questions.correct_answer: Credential lifecycle failure can disable the control plane even when the ledger data structure and cryptography remain intact.
incorrect_answers: A probabilistic blockchain fork can halt channel operations even when every network identity remains fully authorized and functional.
A data privacy leak can permanently halt governance updates even when all other channels are cryptographically secure and operational.
A validator proposal rejection can block future identity renewals and configuration updates from committing later.
questions.explanation: The Fabric lockout example illustrates that certificate renewal and revocation are ongoing security operations, not one-time setup tasks.

questions.question_stem: Two competitors need to share selected shipment proofs with a regulator without exposing all cargo details to each other. Which permissioned-ledger feature best fits this need?
questions.correct_answer: Channels or partitions can limit visibility while preserving shared audit commitments for the relevant parties.
incorrect_answers: Open membership lets every anonymous participant inspect the same transaction details on the ledger.
Deterministic finality automatically encrypts sensitive record fields from unauthorized or competitive auditors.
A single central database is required because permissioned ledgers always expose all data to every network member.
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that permissioned membership does not imply universal visibility; selective channels, partitions, hashes, or commitments can support privacy and auditability.

questions.question_stem: Which compromised identity is most likely to threaten the entire permissioned network's rules rather than only one user's ordinary activity?
questions.correct_answer: An admin identity that can change membership, policies, or configuration.
incorrect_answers: An auditor identity that can only inspect historical blocks and system channels.
A client identity restricted to proposing transactions under static rules.
A read-only user identity that can view one channel state update log.
questions.explanation: The lesson highlights that control-plane credentials have outsized impact because they define who is in the system and which rules apply.

questions.question_stem: In Fabric's execute-order-validate design, why are chaincode proposals executed by endorsing peers before the ordering service sequences the transaction?
questions.correct_answer: Pre-order execution lets endorsers produce signed proposed effects, while later validation can reject mismatches or conflicts without causing all peers to diverge.
incorrect_answers: Pre-order execution lets orderers inspect active application states and evaluate business logic, so consensus can reject invalid transaction results.
Pre-order execution removes the need for cryptographic credentials and membership services, allowing clients to submit proposals to endorsers anonymously.
Pre-order execution purges invalid transactions from peer databases before any permanent audit log or block record can be created by validating peers.
questions.explanation: The reading presents execute-order-validate as Fabric's response to permissioned smart-contract requirements, especially non-determinism, endorsement policy, and modular ordering.

questions.question_stem: A Fabric deployment has one ordering service that establishes block order, but a chaincode policy requires endorsements from two specific organizations before an asset transfer is valid. What distinction is being used?
questions.correct_answer: Ordering-service trust determines transaction order, while endorsement policy determines which organizations must vouch for application-specific effects.
incorrect_answers: Ordering-service trust approves asset ownership updates, while endorsing peers are only responsible for gossiping finalized blocks across the channels.
Endorsement policy replaces cryptographic membership credentials, while identities are completely unnecessary once ordering services establish blocks.
Consensus coordination across all channels guarantees block delivery, while application-level validation ensures that every member approves every block.
questions.explanation: The reading emphasizes that Fabric separates consensus trust from application trust: orderers create a per-channel total order, while endorsement policies express who must approve chaincode results.
questions.lesson_block: Separation Of Consensus And Application Trust

questions.question_stem: Two Fabric transactions are endorsed using the same version of an asset record. After ordering, the first valid transaction updates that asset. Why might the second transaction appear in the ledger but not change current state?
questions.correct_answer: Validation can mark it invalid because its readset is stale, while the append-only ledger still records the attempted transaction for auditability.
incorrect_answers: The ordering service deletes the second transaction from the block, while the append-only state store only records successful updates to avoid database bloat.
Endorsement systems force the second transaction to commit automatically, while subsequent validation checks always bypass stale readset version conflicts.
The peer merges both concurrent writes into one state update, while every channel shares the same global transaction ordering sequence.
questions.explanation: The reading distinguishes the ledger record from current state: invalid transactions can remain audit-visible, but validation prevents their effects from updating versioned state.
